definition: Tantamount means equivalent in effect to something graver.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word tantamount. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know tantamount should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In the old harbor code, dimming your lamp at night was tantamount to piracy.
Akin claims far less than tantamount — the two things merely resemble each other, kinship noted, and there the claim ends.
Equivalent stops short of tantamount — equivalents match in measure or effect, neutrally; tantamount passes a verdict, declaring that the act amounts to the graver thing itself.

Equal is the plain word for two things matching in measure — equal shares, equal weight. It compares amounts and stops there. Tantamount weighs an act against something graver and passes sentence — silence that amounts to consent. Equal counts; tantamount convicts.

As good as is the everyday idiom for the verdict tantamount passes — leaving early was as good as quitting. The idiom belongs to speech and shrugs; tantamount belongs to codes, courts, and editorials, where the equivalence is declared formally and the graver reading is meant to stick.

Tantamount means equivalent in effect to something graver.
On a rope team, the mountaineering manual is blunt.
Unclipping from the line without calling it out, whatever the reason, is tantamount to abandoning your partners — not similar to abandoning them, not a lesser cousin of it.
Guides who unclip silently lose their certification under the same clause as guides who walk away.
Tantamount is the exact word for that clause, because tantamount means equivalent in effect or meaning — the quiet unclip amounts to abandonment even though nobody walked anywhere.
Notice the word's fixed frame: one thing is tantamount to another, and almost always to something grave.
Similar compares; tantamount convicts.
Tantamount lives in one groove: X is tantamount to Y, where Y is graver than X and the sentence is a verdict — silence tantamount to consent, a walkout tantamount to a forfeit.
Equivalent is its neutral cousin for recipes and math; equal is plainer still.
If nothing is being weighed in effect, reach for the neutral word.

When the honor board met in October, the case before it looked small: a junior had glanced at a copied answer sheet during a fire-drill scramble and said nothing afterward.
The student's advocate argued for a warning, reasoning that silence is a lesser act than copying.
The board's chair disagreed and read the code's fourth clause aloud: concealing another student's cheating is tantamount to cheating, and it carries the same penalty.
The clause, he explained, was written after a scandal in which dozens knew and no one spoke; its drafters wanted silence to count as the graver offense itself.
The board voted six to one to apply the clause, and the junior's transcript now bears the same mark a copier's would.
